title: How to move customer training from live sessions to on-demand video
summary: Which customer training sessions to keep live, how to turn the rest into short on-demand videos, and how to measure whether the switch worked.
body_markdown:
Look at your training calendar and find the session nobody would design from scratch today. It's usually the getting-started webinar that runs every week, or the onboarding call each CSM gives every new account, and the trainer could run the first half from memory. That was fine at 50 customers, but at 500 the same hour repeats until it eats the week, and a customer who signs up on Wednesday waits six days to learn the basics.


Live training has a second cost that's easier to miss: each session reaches only the people who showed up. Movable Ink's education team runs instructor-led training alongside self-paced courses in Skilljar, and its[customer story](https://www.clueso.io/customers/movable-ink) describes internal training that "happened live, which meant it reached whoever showed up." When leadership asked to see an hour-long live session on new product initiatives, Shannon Cook, Head of Enablement and Education, put the recording into Clueso and had a five-minute video about 10 minutes later. "It shrunk an hour down to five minutes," she said.


That was one session. A whole program takes more thought, because some of it should stay live. This guide covers which sessions to keep, how to convert the rest, and how to tell whether it worked.


## What does it mean to move customer training to on-demand?


Moving customer training to on-demand means turning the repeatable parts of your live sessions (webinars, onboarding calls, recurring walkthroughs) into short videos and written guides that customers use when they need them. Live training doesn't disappear. It shrinks to the parts that need a conversation, such as questions and account-specific setup.


Posting the webinar recording to your help center doesn't count. A customer who needs to connect one integration won't scrub through 60 minutes to find the four that apply, and as one technical enablement lead told us, "almost nobody sits through unedited webinar recordings." The teams we talk to describe the same target: long live sessions cut into task videos of two to five minutes each. Across more than 26,000 videos exported from Clueso in the past 12 months, with our own team's accounts excluded, the median ran about 1 minute 30 seconds, and 89% came in at five minutes or less.


## Which customer training sessions should stay live?


Ask whether the session changes depending on who attends. Compare the recordings of your last three run-throughs, and the part that overlaps is a video. The part that differs (the questions, the customer's own configuration, the edge cases nobody planned for) is what earns a calendar slot. Our[cluebook chapter on live training](https://www.clueso.io/cluebooks/building-a-customer-education-program--live-training) makes the case for live sessions on those grounds: real-time problem solving, adapting to the audience, and the relationship that comes from talking to a person.


Keep it live


Move it on-demand


Open Q&A and office hours


Product tour and navigation basics


Implementation sessions on the customer's own data and configuration


Standard setup tasks: inviting users, connecting an integration, setting permissions


Deep-dive sessions for power users, where the questions go further than any script


Feature walkthroughs that are the same for every account


Kickoffs with strategic accounts


"What's new" release walkthroughs


Once the basics are on video, the live session that remains can start where the videos stop. One training team we spoke with now has everyone watch the video first and follows up with "a much shorter Q and A session," because "everybody's across the detail."


## How do you decide which sessions to convert first?


One education lead we spoke with counted 88 hours of live training across 37 sessions, and added, "we might deliver the same exact course but to like six different clients." Start by listing every recurring session with how often it runs, how long it lasts, and who delivers it, then multiply those out. A 60-minute onboarding webinar run weekly is 52 hours of presenter time a year before anyone prepares a slide, and the same call run one-to-one by every CSM for every new account costs far more. The sessions with the biggest total and the most repetition go first.


Then read the questions in your Q&A transcripts and support tickets. Questions that come up in every session become videos too, and the ones specific to a single customer are your reason to keep office hours. A ticket about something a session already covered means the customer missed it or forgot it, and a short video at the point of need fixes both. Our guide to[how CSMs build training videos](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-csms-build-training-videos) covers choosing first videos from ticket data.


## How do you turn a recorded live session into short on-demand videos?


If you record your webinars and onboarding calls, you already have the raw material. A live recording needs more cleanup than a planned one, so work through it in this order.


1. **Use the most recent recording.** A polished take from last year shows screens your customers no longer see.
2. **Cut everything that only made sense live.** That means "can everyone see my screen," waiting for latecomers, tangents, and the Q&A block. Save the recurring questions, since each could be its own short video.
3. **Split by task, not by the clock.** Each video should answer one question a customer would type into your help center search, such as "how do I add a teammate?" A ten-minute chunk that happens to fall between two slides is not a module.
4. **Check every frame for what shouldn't leave the room.** Live sessions often run on a real account, with attendee names in the participant panel and customer data on screen. Blur them, or re-record that task on a clean demo account.
5. **Watch each video cold, the way a new customer would.** Out of context, lines like "as I mentioned earlier" stop making sense.


> **Split long recordings in one pass.**[Clueso Cuts](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-cuts) breaks a long recording into titled, described clips from a chat instruction, such as "one clip per task, drop the Q&A," and each clip becomes its own editable project. Clueso then rewrites the script and adds an[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) . Clueso Cuts is on the Enterprise plan.


> **Working from Claude or Cursor?** The[live session to on-demand modules skill](https://www.clueso.io/video-skills/live-session-to-on-demand-modules) runs the same cleanup-then-split workflow through the[Clueso MCP](https://www.clueso.io/mcp) , which is on every plan.


## How should you organize on-demand training so customers find the right video?


Order videos by the customer's path to first value rather than by your product's menu. A new admin needs account setup, user invites, and one core workflow before anything else. If admins and end users do different jobs in your product, give each role its own path. Our[SaaS customer onboarding guide](https://www.clueso.io/blog/saas-customer-onboarding) covers the stages these paths follow, and our[training video library](https://www.clueso.io/blog/training-video-library) post covers the library's structure.


Movable Ink stitches small master clips into longer walkthroughs, so a learner meeting a workflow for the first time sees all five steps while another course shows only steps two to four. Put the videos where customers already look: the help center article, the in-app help menu, and the academy course. Pair each video with a written guide for customers who would rather skim, and for the AI support assistants that answer from your documentation.


> **One recording, two formats.** Every Clueso video also produces a[step-by-step written guide](https://www.clueso.io/features/help-articles) with screenshots, and videos[embed anywhere](https://www.clueso.io/features/embed-videos-anywhere) with a link or a code snippet.


> **Running an academy in an LMS?**[SCORM export](https://www.clueso.io/features/scorm-export) (SCORM 1.2, SCORM 2004, and xAPI) and in-video quizzes are on the Enterprise plan. When a video changes, Publish update refreshes the course in your LMS without a re-upload.


## How do you keep on-demand training accurate when the product changes?


A live trainer can talk around a renamed button, but a video keeps showing the old one, and customers who follow outdated steps open tickets. One task per video means a changed screen costs one short fix. Movable Ink's customer education lead put it this way: "If something changes in step one or step two, we just change that clip and it gets pushed everywhere." Our post on how to[update a training video without re-recording](https://www.clueso.io/blog/update-training-video-without-re-recording) covers the mechanics.


## How do you know the move to on-demand is working?


Measure what your live sessions were supposed to achieve: time to first value for new accounts, completion of the onboarding path, support tickets on the topics you converted, and the presenter hours your team gets back. Compare accounts onboarded after the switch with those onboarded live the quarter before. If time to first value holds steady while presenter hours fall, the move worked.


Completion alone can mislead, because a finished video doesn't prove the customer did the task. Teamworks, whose academy runs at 90% video content, tracks completion against what people actually do in the product afterward ([customer story](https://www.clueso.io/customers/teamworks) ). Our[customer education metrics chapter](https://www.clueso.io/cluebooks/building-a-customer-education-program--metrics-to-track) lists more measures.


Some sessions stay live for a reason that has nothing to do with teaching: they're the only way to prove who was trained. An enablement lead told us a colleague keeps defaulting to live sessions "because at least I can tell. I can check these people have had the training." Completion tracking in an LMS answers that question without a calendar slot.


> **See what gets watched.** Viewership analytics are on Clueso's Business and Enterprise plans. Compare plans on the[pricing page](https://www.clueso.io/pricing) .


## Frequently asked questions


### How do you reduce live training sessions without hurting onboarding?


Convert the sessions that repeat word for word, and keep live time for questions and account-specific setup. In Clueso, one recording becomes a video and a[step-by-step guide](https://www.clueso.io/features/help-articles) , so each converted session ships as both.


### Can on-demand video replace live training sessions?


It can replace the repeatable parts, but not the conversation: office hours, implementation sessions on a customer's own data, and deep dives with power users still work better live. If your old sessions are recorded,[Clueso Cuts](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-cuts) (Enterprise plan) splits them into short task videos from a chat instruction.


### Our CSMs spend half their week on training calls. What fixes that?


Turn the parts every customer hears into a short video path the CSM sends before the first call, so the call starts on the customer's own setup. CSMs can build the videos themselves: they record the task once, and Clueso writes the script, adds an[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) , zooms, and captions, and produces the written guide.


### How long should an on-demand customer training video be?


Long enough to finish one task, which for most product tasks is two to five minutes. A topic that runs past five minutes is usually two tasks. Short clips also make updates cheaper, because Clueso lets you edit one clip's script and[regenerate its voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) without re-recording the rest.


## How to start converting your live training this week


Pick the session that ran most often last quarter and open its latest recording. Mark every point where the trainer says something they say in every session. Those timestamps are your first module list, and the questions in the Q&A at the end tell you what the live session that replaces it should cover.
